Confusable pairs among impairment, distraction and drowsiness rules, where similar-sounding limits apply to different drivers or substances; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec10-R01 | anchor: A01
The 0.00% alcohol limit is the rule for drivers under 21, while for controlled substances any amount counts as impaired regardless of the driver's age. [A01]
Why it matters: group impairment; confusable alcohol limit versus controlled substance rule.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-R02 | anchor: A01
A medicine being legal to buy or prescribed to you does not make it legal to drive on, since driving under the influence of any drug is illegal. [A01]
Why it matters: group impairment; misconception prescribed means safe to drive.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-R03 | anchor: A01
Refusing a PAC test leads to arrest under the Implied Consent Law and a loss of driving privileges for at least one year, so refusal is not a way out. [A01]
Why it matters: group implied consent; misconception refusing avoids penalties.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-R04 | anchor: A01
A PAC test can be either a breathalyzer test or a blood test. [A01]
Why it matters: group implied consent; confusable breath versus blood test.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-R05 | anchor: A01
Permit and probationary license holders may use a phone while driving only to report an emergency, while regular license holders are told to avoid it and use hands-free if they must. [A01]
Why it matters: group phones; confusable permit or probationary versus regular license.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-R06 | anchor: A01
The headphone rule covers headsets or headphones that cover or go in both ears, and the radio rule is about keeping the volume low enough to hear emergency vehicles. [A01]
Why it matters: group distraction; confusable headphones versus radio volume.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-R07 | anchor: A01
Answering a phone is something to avoid while moving; the handbook's alternative is to pull over safely before using it. [A01]
Why it matters: group phones; prereq safe stopping.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec10-R08 | anchor: A02
Reading directions and eating are both tasks for a parked or pulled-over car, not for driving. [A02]
Why it matters: group distraction; misconception quick glances are fine.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec10-R09 | anchor: A02
Drowsiness can come from an untreated sleep disorder or a long work shift, not only from a short night's sleep. [A02]
Why it matters: group drowsy driving; misconception only lack of sleep matters.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec10-R10 | anchor: A02
Drifting from your lane and hitting the rumble strip are drowsiness warning signs that call for pulling over to rest, just like frequent yawning or blinking. [A02]
Why it matters: group drowsy driving; confusable warning signs.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]
